strengths: Addresses a clear and well-motivated gap: PVGs (Merlin-Arthur classifiers) do not scale to high-dimensional images, while CBMs are often restricted to linear classifiers with an interpretability-accuracy gap; combining the two via concept-space prover-verifier games is a sensible and underexplored idea.

Extensive experimental evaluation spanning synthetic (CLEVR-Hans3/7) and large-scale real-world datasets (CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1k, COCOLogic), with multiple concept extractors (NCB, CLIP/SpLiCE), several baselines (ResNet, Pixel-MAC, linear/nonlinear CBM, DCR), and thorough ablations (mask size, γ weighting, prover/verifier architecture) in the supplementary material.

Strong quantitative results: NCV attains near-perfect soundness alongside competitive or superior completeness relative to Pixel-MAC and CBM baselines across all tested datasets, and scales to ImageNet-1k where Pixel-MAC essentially fails.
Qualitative comparisons (Fig. 3, Fig. 4) convincingly show that concept-level explanations are more human-interpretable than the diffuse pixel masks produced by Pixel-MAC.

Unusually candid and detailed theoretical appendix (Suppl. A) that explicitly discusses the gap between the idealized binary Merlin-Arthur guarantees and the paper's high-dimensional, multi-class, sparse-concept setting, including why average precision/mutual-information bounds cannot be reliably estimated in practice — this is a commendable transparency about limitations rather than overclaiming.
Practical computational cost analysis (Suppl. F) showing NCV is 1-3 orders of magnitude cheaper than Pixel-MAC and comparable to standard CBMs, supporting the scalability claim.
Shortcut-learning experiments on CLEVR-Hans with varying amounts of clean data show consistent improvements in validation-test gap over CBM baselines.
weaknesses: The abstract and main text advertise 'formal verifiability' and 'information-theoretic guarantees,' but the paper's own supplementary material (Sec. A.5) admits that in the actual multi-class, high-dimensional, sparse-concept regime used in experiments, the precision/mutual-information bounds cannot be meaningfully estimated, the AFC/relative-success-rate/class-imbalance parameters are not measured, and the one-vs-rest reduction does not cover the joint K-class decision. This creates a mismatch between the strength of claims in the main paper and what is actually substantiated, which is a soundness concern.

The core technical contribution is largely a direct application of the existing Merlin-Arthur framework (Wäldchen et al., 2024) to concept vectors instead of pixels, plus engineering choices (rejection-class loss modification, continuous-to-discrete mask training). The conceptual novelty beyond this combination is limited.

Comparisons with Pixel-MAC may be somewhat unfair: Pixel-MAC uses fixed hyperparameters across vastly different dataset scales (e.g., same U-Net/mask configuration philosophy for CIFAR-100 and ImageNet), and its extremely low completeness (e.g., 15% on CIFAR-100) suggests it may be undertrained or poorly tuned rather than fundamentally incapable, making the reported gap potentially inflated.

Interpretability/explanation quality (Q3) is assessed only qualitatively via a handful of examples (Fig. 3, Fig. 4); there is no quantitative or human-subject evaluation of explanation faithfulness, completeness, or usefulness, despite this being a central motivating claim of the paper.

The concept vocabulary quality is not independently validated — CLIP/SpLiCE-derived concepts inherit biases and can diverge from expert semantics (as the discussion section itself notes, citing Debole et al. 2025), yet no quantitative concept-quality metric is reported to contextualize how this affects the verifiability claims.

The mechanistic explanation for why NCV mitigates shortcut learning better than nonlinear CBM is not established causally; it is plausible that any sparsification/masking mechanism (not specifically the adversarial prover-verifier game) drives the improvement, and no ablation isolates the adversarial component's specific contribution to shortcut robustness.

Mask size (e.g., 12 of 64 concepts, 32 of 10k concepts) appears to be a sensitive, dataset-specific hyperparameter requiring manual tuning (as shown in Suppl. D/E ablations), raising concerns about generalizability to new datasets without extensive tuning.

strengths: Well-motivated combination of two complementary but previously disjoint lines of work: Prover-Verifier Games/Merlin-Arthur classifiers (formal verifiability) and concept-based models (interpretability for high-dimensional inputs), addressing genuine scalability and expressivity limitations of each.

Broad and fairly rigorous empirical evaluation spanning synthetic (CLEVR-Hans3/7) and real-world, large-scale datasets (CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1k, COCOLogic), with multiple seeds and standard deviations reported throughout.

Strong supplementary ablations (mask size, choice of prover/verifier architecture, weighting parameter γ, and an additional comparison against Deep Concept Reasoning) that substantiate design choices and show NCV scales where a strong nonlinear interpretable baseline (DCR) fails to complete training on ImageNet-1k.
The shortcut-learning experiment (Table 2) is a nice controlled study showing NCV's validation-test gap shrinks faster than CBM baselines as clean data increases, supporting the robustness claim.

The paper is unusually candid about the limits of its own theoretical claims (Suppl. A.5): it explicitly notes that the Merlin-Arthur mutual-information bounds are not empirically estimated due to high-dimensional sparsity, class imbalance in one-vs-rest reductions, and unverified relative success rate of the adversarial prover, and treats completeness/soundness as proxies rather than certified guarantees — this is good scientific practice rather than overclaiming.

Reported computational cost comparison (Suppl. F) demonstrates NCV is substantially cheaper than pixel-based MAC and comparable to standard CBMs, supporting the scalability claim with concrete numbers.
Clear writing, good figures contrasting pixel-level vs. concept-level explanations (Fig. 3, 4) that intuitively convey the interpretability benefit.
weaknesses: The core novelty is largely a systems-level combination of two existing frameworks (Merlin-Arthur classifiers and pretrained concept extractors such as NCB/SpLiCE) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; the prover/verifier/extractor components are all adapted from prior work.

The formal verifiability claims are substantially weakened by the honest admission that the theoretical bounds (average precision, mutual information, AFC κ, class imbalance B, relative success rate α) are never estimated in the experiments; readers are asked to interpret completeness/soundness as an 'idealised lens' rather than certified guarantees, which somewhat undercuts the headline framing of 'formal verifiability' and 'pushing towards real-world verifiability.'

The claim that NCV 'narrows or closes' the interpretability-accuracy gap is not fully supported: on ImageNet-1k, NCV (67.04) actually underperforms the nonlinear CBM baseline (69.02), which is acknowledged but somewhat undercuts the generality of the Q2 answer.

Explanation quality for the CLIP-based instantiation is uneven — the qualitative ImageNet example ('mugs and cups and extend and support and cappuchino') mixes coherent and seemingly irrelevant/noisy concept tokens, raising questions about how consistently human-interpretable the CLIP/SpLiCE-derived vocabulary is in practice, despite the paper's claim of 'meaningful' explanations.

Soundness of NCV is fundamentally tied to the strength of the trained Morgana prover (a specific neural architecture), and the paper does not empirically probe adversarial robustness against stronger/alternative adversaries or out-of-distribution attacks on the concept masks, so the 'soundness' guarantee is only as strong as the specific adversary used during training.

Shortcut-learning mitigation is only demonstrated on the synthetic CLEVR-Hans benchmark with an engineered spurious correlation; it is unclear whether the same benefits would hold for naturally occurring, real-world spurious correlations in the CIFAR-100/ImageNet/COCOLogic settings, which limits the generality of the Q4 claim.

The dependency on frozen, pretrained concept extractors means NCV inherits any biases, entanglement, or vocabulary limitations of NCB/CLIP-SpLiCE; while acknowledged as a limitation, this is a significant practical bottleneck for real-world deployment that is not stress-tested (e.g., no experiments varying concept-extractor quality).
